_readme: A catalogue of real, widely-available watches, used to seed the pending queue
WHAT THIS IS: brand, model reference and specification, written from general
knowledge of these models. Nothing here was scraped, and no price is stored -
prices change and a stale price breaches the Associates terms.
WHAT THIS IS NOT: verified. Model references get revised, specifications vary
between regional variants, and knowledge of a specific reference can be out of
date. Every field arrives flagged as an unreviewed draft and the approve gate
will not let a watch through until a human has confirmed it against the real
listing. Treat this as a well-informed starting point, not a source of truth.
`confidence` is how sure the writer is of the stated specification:
high   - iconic, stable model, specification unlikely to be wrong
medium - well known, but variants differ; check the exact reference
Fields left null are genuinely unknown. The copy engine turns a missing fact
into an honest caveat rather than a guess, so null is better than a bad value.

watches.note: The default cheap digital watch. Alarm, stopwatch, backlight, resin strap. 30 m means rain and handwashing, not swimming.
Steel bracelet version of the classic Casio digital. Same electronics as the F-91W in a metal case.
Long-standing budget diver recommendation. Genuine 200 m rating and a rotating bezel at a price that usually buys neither.
Slip-through strap, Indiglo backlight. Reference varies by strap colour; confirm the exact one.
Plain high-contrast field dial with Indiglo. Several strap and dial variants share the Scout name.
Larger digital with a 100 m rating and a 10-year battery. Confirm the case measurement, which is quoted inconsistently.
7S26 movement: no hand-winding and no hacking seconds. The standard first mechanical watch, and small by modern standards at 37 mm.
SKX-shaped case with a 4R36 movement, which hand-winds and hacks. 100 m, not the 200 m of the SKX it resembles - worth being clear about.
Domed crystal, applied indices, thin bezel. Bambino references change often between versions and dial colours; confirm the exact one.
Sapphire crystal and 200 m at a price where mineral glass is the norm. F6922 movement hacks and hand-winds.
Analogue-digital, carbon core guard, octagonal bezel. Thin for a G-Shock. Case width is quoted several ways; 45.4 mm includes the guards.
Light-powered, so no battery changes and no winding. Small, plain, and hard to argue with as an everyday watch.
Unusual compression case design that seals harder under pressure. Finishing is rough and the bezel is loose by design; that is the point, not a fault.
Smaller Mako variant. References in this family are numerous and easily confused; confirm case size and crystal before publishing.
Cushion case that wears smaller than 45 mm suggests because of the short lugs. ISO-rated 200 m. 4R36 movement.
ISO-rated solar diver. Crystal is mineral on most references in this family, not sapphire - worth checking, because it is often described wrongly.
Sunburst textured dial under a domed crystal. Crystal material differs across Cocktail Time references; confirm before claiming sapphire.
Hand-wound H-50 with a long power reserve. No rotor, so it is thin. A genuine military-pattern field watch rather than a styling exercise.
Integrated bracelet, Powermatic 80 movement with roughly 80 hours of reserve. A quartz version exists at a much lower price - do not conflate them.
Automatic H-10 with a long reserve. Sold in 38 mm and 42 mm; confirm which reference the listing is for.
6R35 movement, roughly 70 hours of reserve, sapphire crystal. Modern reinterpretation of the 1965 diver, and notably thick.
Powermatic 80 movement and a 300 m rating. Reference numbers in this family are long and easily mistyped; confirm carefully.
300 m, ceramic bezel on newer references. Many variants share the HydroConquest name across sizes and movements.
Larger 7S36 field watch with day-date and 100 m. No hand-winding or hacking, as with all 7S movements.
